title: The Gadget Gala Code Crackers
markdown:
The sun didn’t just peek through Callum’s window; it burst in, painting the room with streaks of brilliant red, orange, and yellow. Today was the Fantastic Gadget Gala, and Callum, whose fingers could dance like quicksilver on any circuit board, practically sprang from his bed. His backpack, a trusty canvas friend, felt light and ready, stuffed with springs, screws, and bits of gleaming wire. He grabbed his lucky toolkit, a polished tin box that clicked open with a satisfying snap.

Outside, the town square buzzed. The Gala tent rose like a giant colourful castle, its fabric flapping in the cool morning air. Tiny blinking gadgets on top winked like excited fireflies. Inside, the air hummed with chatter and the whirring of amazing inventions. Little robots zipped past, offering tiny cupcakes, and a spectacular contraption juggled glowing orbs. But a tricky puzzling problem had popped up. The grand prize, a Super-Duper Auto-Scribbler that could draw anything you imagined, was locked behind a giant digital number display. Nobody could crack the code. Numbers flashed and flickered: 7, 12, 5, 9, 14, 8, 6, 11, 10, 7.

Callum’s brow furrowed under his smudged spectacles. He pushed them up his nose with a grimy finger. “It’s no good,” he declared, tapping the paper where he’d scribbled the numbers. “I’ve tried everything. The numbers just don’t make sense.” He’d added them all up and divided by how many there were. “That’s the average, the mean,” he explained to the host, a flustered man whose bowtie kept trying to escape. “It came out to 9. But the code isn’t 9.” He’d lined them up neatly, too. “The middle number, the median, was 9.5. Still no luck.” The host wrung his hands. “Oh dear, oh dear,” he wailed, voice cracking.

Suddenly a streak of brown fur zipped past. It was Birch, the squirrel who could sort acorns by size, colour, and shininess with astonishing speed. He skidded to a halt, bushy tail flicking like a tiny flag. “Callum. I’m trying to share my acorn treasure with my cousins,” he chattered, nose twitching. “I have ten, but they’re all different sizes. It’s tricky to make it fair.” He held up a paw. “See? This one is tiny, perfect for a little snack. This one is mighty.” He pointed to a plump acorn, almost as big as his paw. “And I have two medium-sized ones, just about right for a hungry belly.”

“Sharing is tough when things aren’t the same,” Callum mused, tapping a finger on his chin, leaving a faint grey smudge. He looked at the prize numbers again. “We have ten of them: 7, 12, 5, 9, 14, 8, 6, 11, 10, and 7.” He scribbled them down again. “The mean is 9. The median is 9.5. But the prize code is a three-digit number, and it’s stuck.”

Just then Mrs. Rowan, the wisest owl from the Whispering Woods Library, glided in. She landed on a nearby shelf, movements as smooth as rippling water. Her feathery spectacles gleamed on her beak. “Ah, Callum,” she hooted softly, voice like the rustle of old pages. “Sometimes the best way to understand a collection of things is to look at them in different ways. Just as Birch finds different ways to appreciate his acorns.”

Birch, ever observant, pointed to his acorns. “When I sort them,” he chattered, “I see the smallest ones, the biggest ones, and the ones that are most common. Like, I have two medium-sized ones.” He demonstrated by lining up a few acorns. “See? These two are the same. They’re the most in my pile.”

Callum’s eyes widened. “Most common. That’s the mode. The number that pops up the most.” He scanned the prize numbers. “Let’s see… 7, 12, 5, 9, 14, 8, 6, 11, 10, 7.” He circled the two sevens with a bold stroke. “The number 7 appears twice. All the others only appear once.”

“The mode is 7,” Birch squeaked, bouncing with excitement.

“But the prize code is a three-digit number,” Callum fretted, pacing a small circle. “Seven isn’t three digits.”

Mrs. Rowan blinked her big wise eyes. “What if,” she suggested gently, “you needed to find the middle number when the numbers were all neat and tidy? Think of your acorns, Birch. If you lined them up from smallest to biggest, what would be the one right in the middle?”

Callum scrambled for his paper. “Order the numbers. Yes.” He quickly rearranged the prize numbers from smallest to largest: 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14. He counted them carefully. Ten numbers. “So there isn’t one single middle number,” he declared, a hint of disappointment in his voice. “There are two in the middle: 8 and 9.”

“When there are two middle numbers,” Mrs. Rowan explained, voice a soft rustle, “we can find the number exactly between them. What number sits perfectly between 8 and 9?”

“8.5,” Birch squeaked, whiskers quivering.

“But that’s not a whole number,” Callum protested, tapping his pencil against the digital display. “The prize code has to be whole numbers.”

“Exactly,” Mrs. Rowan hooted, a twinkle in her eye. “What if the puzzle needs a different approach? What if you consider the numbers without the most common one?”

Callum paused, his energetic mind slowing. He looked at his neat list again: 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14. The mode was 7. What if they ignored one of the sevens? He carefully rewrote the remaining numbers, leaving out one 7: 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14. Now there were eight numbers. “The middle numbers are 9 and 10,” Callum said, voice ringing with discovery. “The number between them is 9.5.” He slumped slightly. “Still not a code.”

“Perhaps,” Mrs. Rowan whispered, “the puzzle requires a different perspective. What if you used the median of the original list of numbers, but rounded up?”

Callum’s mind whirred like a tiny motor. The original list: 7, 12, 5, 9, 14, 8, 6, 11, 10, 7. The median was 9.5. “Round up?” he whispered, fingers flying across the notepad. He pictured the Auto-Scribbler. He tentatively entered 957. Nothing. A harsh red X flashed. He tried 795. Another red X. He looked at the number of digits for the prize. It was three. He looked at the mode again: 7. The median of the other numbers after removing the 7s was 9.5.

Callum’s heart thumped a frantic rhythm against his ribs. He lined up the numbers again: 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14. The mode was 7. He looked at the numbers around the remaining 7. He had 6 on one side and 8 on the other. The middle number between 6 and 8? That was 7. That didn’t make sense for a three-digit code.

“Wait,” Birch chattered, tail giving an excited twitch. He pointed a tiny paw towards Callum’s carefully ordered list. “What if the prize code is made from the smallest number, the most common number, and the median number of the other numbers, the ones left over?”

Callum looked at his neat list: 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14.
Smallest: 5.
Most common, the mode: 7.
The numbers other than the two 7s were: 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14. The median of this set was 9.5. What if he rounded that up to 10? But 10 isn’t a single digit.

“What if,” Callum whispered, eyes shining, “it’s the smallest number, the mode, and then the rounded-up median of the remaining numbers, but we only use the last digit of that median number if it’s two digits?” The smallest is 5. The mode is 7. The median of the remaining is 9.5, rounded up is 10. The last digit of 10 is 0.

“Five, seven, zero,” Birch squeaked, bouncing on the balls of his tiny feet.

Callum’s fingers flew across the keypad, a blur of motion. 5 – 7 – 0.

Beep. The giant screen flashed a brilliant vibrant green. Success. The lock clicked open with a satisfying thunk, a sound that echoed through the silent tent. The Super-Duper Auto-Scribbler gleamed under the lights, its metallic surfaces reflecting the excited faces all around.

A huge cheer erupted. Callum grinned, smudged glasses practically sparkling with triumph. He scooped Birch onto his shoulder. Mrs. Rowan hooted, wings giving a little flap of applause. Mean, median, and mode had each given them a different look at the same pile of numbers, the way Birch’s acorns could be tiny, mighty, or simply the ones that showed up twice. The Auto-Scribbler waited. Callum, who never could resist a circuit, already wondered what it would draw first: a squirrel, an owl, or a keypad that finally said yes.
characters: Callum (a quicksilver gadget fixer), Birch (an acorn-sorting squirrel), Mrs. Rowan (a wise library owl)
